newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq threatened with new sanctions from UN Council.
newsitem.headline: Iraq threatened with new sanctions from UN Council.

text.p: The United Nations Security Council has adopted a resolution threatening Iraq with further sanctions if it does not allow U.N. arms inspectors to search sensitive sites.

The resolution, approved by a unanimous vote late on Saturday expresses the council's "firm intention to impose additional measures" on Iraqi officials responsible for barring the U.N. arms inspectors from the sites.
The vote came after a deal was struck between President Clinton and Russia's Boris Yeltsin at the Group of Seven summit of industrial nations in Denver that averted a Russian veto.

The resolution also suspends regular Council reviews of sanctions against Iraq, usually held every 60 days, until the end of October, two weeks after the arms inspectors report again on Iraqi compliance.
Unless the inspectors are satisfied, stringent sanctions against Iraq, particularly oil exports, cannot be lifted. The embargoes were imposed in 1990 after Baghdad invaded Kuwait.

U.N. inspectors, looking for weapons of mass destruction and related materials, were prevented from searching three sites on June 10 and 12. Iraq has argued it could bar them from areas dealing with national security.

The resolution, however, postpones differences in the council until October when, in the words of British Ambassador Sir John Weston, "it points firmly towards taking additional measures against Iraq."

But a new resolution would be needed to impose any further sanctions, such as a travel ban on Iraqi officials responsible for blocking the inspections. Egypt, Russia and China have indicated they had reservations on enacting new sanctions.

Although the final text was weaker than the United States and Britain first proposed, both nations were satisfied that the council took a tougher position than it has over the last year. Russia had threatened to veto their original text while France and China would have abstained.
All three countries along with the United States and Britain are permanent members of the council with veto power.

But Iraq's ambassador Nizar Hamdoon considered the final document too harsh. "There is less poison than there was before but it is still poisonous. That's my way of describing the text," he told reporters.

A senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Yeltsin had agreed to "accept the principle of new sanctions" after his conversation with Clinton in Denver on how to prevent "rogue states seeking to develop weapons of mass destruction."
Originally the United States and Britain wanted immediate travel sanctions on the military as well as certain government departments responsible for blocking the inspections.

Russia's U.N. ambassador Sergei Lavrov, repeatedly stressed to reporters that the new text imposed no new sanctions. He said the United States and Britain had wanted to introduce a range of sanctions "that would cover even secretaries and cleaners and the like."
But he said "this resolution is to send a strong signal from the council" to make sure U.N. inspectors could complete their work so the oil embargo could be lifted.
